title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Thames and the Dust

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.

Over the course of this series, we'll be moving through the novel chapter by chapter — its dust heaps and river, its frauds and its tenderness, its extraordinary gallery of human vanity and human goodness.
I'm joined today by three guests whose different ways of reading make for the kind of conversation Dickens himself would have relished.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing professor whose great subject is craft — how a novelist builds meaning through structure, image, and the grain of a sentence.
There are few readers I know who can make close reading feel as thrilling as Eleanor does.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of great fiction — character under pressure, goodness tested, the individual soul.
Edmund reads Dickens against the grain of received opinion, and the result is always bracing.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and arguably the greatest living reader of Victorian fiction aloud — brings to every page the instincts of a performer.
He hears what's written for the voice, and he makes you hear it too.
We begin today where the novel begins — in the mud and the money, the Thames and the dust.
But I want to open with something that comes a little later — a passage about Bella Wilfer, and the question the novel keeps asking about all of us.
What do we really want — and what does that wanting say about who we are?
Bella Wilfer is one of the great achievements of this novel, and I think she's underestimated.
She's funny — genuinely, sharply funny — in a way that Dickens usually reserves for his comic grotesques.
But she's also the novel's conscience in embryo.
There's a passage that crystallises this perfectly — Bella alone in her room after a conversation with Mr Boffin, interrogating herself in the looking-glass.
She thinks to herself: 'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself.'
And then: 'Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
And finally she turns on herself: 'Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That word — 'Beast' — is extraordinary.
It's comic, it's self-lacerating, and it's the voice of someone genuinely beginning to know herself.
I'm glad you've begun there, Eleanor, because I think that scene goes to the heart of what the novel is actually about.
Not the dust heaps, not the Thames — though they are magnificent — but the question of whether a human soul can recognise its own corruption and turn from it.
What's striking to me is the precision of the moral anatomy here.
Bella knows the truth of what Boffin has said — she even assents to it — and yet she resents him for saying it.
That is not satire — that is something older, and more serious.
Johnson would have called it the corruption of self-love disguising itself as appetite for the world.
Edmund is right about the moral weight, but I want to insist on the comedy too — because the comedy is doing the moral work.
When I read this aloud, the line that stops audiences every time is the poke.

There's a later passage where Bella is listening to Lizzie Hexam speak of selfless love, and Dickens writes — with complete deadpan precision — that she gives herself 'a penitential poke in the side.'
But what leads to the poke is this: 'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
The fact that she's talking to herself, scolding herself, physically punishing herself — that is Dickens writing character from the inside.
It's also genuinely hilarious, which is why it works as redemption.
And what's so remarkable is that the very same scene gives us Lizzie Hexam at her most luminous — as a kind of counter-example to everything Bella is struggling with.
Lizzie speaks of Eugene Wrayburn — a man she knows she shouldn't love, who can offer her almost nothing — and what she says is devastating in its simplicity.
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
That phrase — 'the light of them' — referring to his eyes — is one of the most quietly beautiful things in the whole novel.
It costs her nothing to say it, and yet we feel it costs her everything.
That is the novel's great contrast, isn't it — Bella measuring everything against what it can fetch, and Lizzie willing to forgo any return at all.
And what's instructive is that Dickens does not make it easy.
Lizzie's selflessness is not presented as a kind of comfortable virtue — it is shown to be genuinely painful, carried alone.
She says, and it's worth noting this, that before Bella arrived she had no thought of parting with a single word of it.
This is a woman who has been carrying an entire interior world in silence.
And that's what makes the scene land — because Dickens gives us the exact moment the wall comes down.
Lizzie tells Bella: 'you came in, and my mind changed.'
Four words.
On the page that barely registers.
Read aloud — with the weight of everything that's come before it — it's crushing.
So already in these early passages we have the novel's two registers sounding at once — the comic and the devastating, sometimes in the same breath.
And both grounded in character — in the inner life that Dickens renders with such extraordinary intimacy.
We'll be returning to Bella and to Lizzie throughout this series.
But next, we turn to the world that shapes them — the river, the dust heaps, and the extraordinary opening chapters of the novel.

segments.title: Bella's Bargain: Money, Love, and Self-Deception

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Charles Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with all the time the book deserves.

I'm your host, and today we're diving deep into one of the novel's most morally intricate threads: Bella Wilfer, her relationship with money, and the strange theatrical machinery Dickens builds around her transformation.
With me are three guests whose company I'd want for exactly this kind of conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher whose great obsession is craft — the architecture of sentences, the structural decision that makes a chapter cohere.
She is precisely the reader you want when Dickens is doing something technically audacious.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral investigations — stories of individual character tested, weakened, or redeemed by circumstance.
He is, as ever, politely resistant to any reading that turns a novel into a political pamphlet.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice of more classic audiobooks than any living person — comes to every novel as a performer first, hearing what the prose does in the mouth before he asks what it means on the page.
Today's question is this: what is Dickens actually doing with Bella Wilfer and money — and does the answer satisfy?
What strikes me first is how Dickens separates the problem of money into two distinct registers — the psychological and the theatrical.
On the psychological side you have John Harmon, who is perhaps the most genuinely conflicted figure in the novel when it comes to inherited wealth.
His great confession passage is remarkable for the way it loops and doubles back on itself — as though the character must audit his own conscience in real time.
The setup is so careful:
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — is doing enormous structural work.
It isn't rhetorical ornament; it's Dickens enacting the psychology of a man who cannot advance without first circling back.
That's well observed, Eleanor, and I'd press it a little further.
What Dickens is really tracing in Harmon is the corruption of the moral imagination by a tainted inheritance — not by capitalism in the abstract, but by one man's specific, poisoning will.
Harmon concludes that passage with a moment of almost Johnsonian self-examination — he addresses himself directly: 'Is that so? That is exactly so.'
That is the voice of a conscience in good order — unflinching about its own history.
The novel's moral interest, for me, is always here: not in the social system, but in whether the individual soul can achieve that clarity.
Edmund's right about the self-examination, but what I hear in that passage — as a performer — is the exhaustion.
The prose actually runs short of breath by the end: 'timid, divided in my mind, afraid of myself and everybody here.'
Those three brief phrases, stacked without conjunctions — that's not Dickens being rhetorical, that's a man who has run out of ways to escape his own history.
And then the deception compounds, as the next chapter makes heartbreakingly clear.
Yes — and the passage from the following chapter is where the structural analysis of the deception is most beautifully laid out.

Dickens writes of how Harmon 'lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
That phrase — accumulative power of its separate circumstances — is one of the great psychological formulations in the entire novel.
It describes moral drift with clinical precision — the way no single step seems decisive, and yet the destination becomes irreversible.
And the impossible bind Harmon finds himself in is stated with admirable economy.
Dickens gives us the dilemma entire — and you must hear it whole to feel its force:
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
That is a genuine moral antinomy — not a false dilemma constructed for plot, but a real one about the dignity of persons.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood of political life — that the tragic situations are those where every available action corrupts something.
And into this moral labyrinth of Harmon's making steps Bella herself — watched by a man she doesn't know loves her.
Oliver, there's a passage where Rokesmith — still in his disguise — simply observes Bella from a doorway, and I'd like you to take us to it.
It's one of those moments where Dickens writes almost as a stage direction — purely visual, purely still.
Here is what Dickens gives us:

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
The genius is in the contrast Dickens constructs without comment: youth watched in silence; old age trudging away with no one watching at all.
And 'boofer lady' — that's Johnny's baby name for Bella, borrowed by the narrator without explanation.
It makes Rokesmith's gaze tender rather than predatory — a man in love, not a man surveilling.
What I'd add is that Dickens places Betty Higden's exit — away from paralysis and pauperism — as the counter-image to Bella's romantic situation.
Both women are escaping something: Betty escapes the workhouse; Bella, we hope, will escape the workhouse of her own mercenary ambitions.
Dickens is too subtle to underline it — he simply places the images side by side, and trusts us.
Let's turn to what Bella is actually being taught — and by whom — because Mr Boffin's role in her education is one of the novel's strangest and most debated mechanisms.
Edmund, I wonder if you'd like to start here — because the question of whether Boffin's corruption is real or performed goes right to the heart of what Dickens is morally arguing.
The novel asks us to believe two irreconcilable things simultaneously, and that is either its greatest audacity or its most significant flaw.
What Bella sees — and what the narration appears to confirm — is genuinely disturbing.
Dickens writes of what she perceives when she dares to look:
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
Those are not the qualities of a good man playing a villain — they are the classical attributes of a soul under corruption.
To be told retrospectively that it was all a loving performance tests the moral imagination rather severely.
Edmund, as someone who has performed villains and benevolent deceivers in equal measure, I find the Boffin problem genuinely fascinating.
The scene where he counsels Bella is written with such relish — it can only be played as great comic villainy, real or performed.
Listen to the rhythm when he tells her to go in for money:
'Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.'
And then that final, shuddering repetition — 'R—r—rich!' — written with the stammer of avarice actually on the page.
Whether Boffin believes it or not, Dickens absolutely believes in how it sounds — and how it corrupts the ear that receives it.
And there's a wonderful satirical detour in the same section that shows Dickens hasn't lost his comic footing while all this moral drama unfolds.
Boffin's rant about charity titles is one of the funniest passages in this part of the novel — and the funniest things in Dickens always carry the sharpest edge.
He surveys the pretension of philanthropic giving:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The escalating absurdity of the titles — deceased patrons, ex-vice-patronesses — is pure Dickensian list comedy.
But it also places Rokesmith — our disguised Harmon — at the centre of institutional hypocrisy about charity, which is the very thing his father's money has made him heir to.
The point is well taken, Eleanor, though I'd note that Boffin's outrage is entirely moral in register — not political.
He objects not to the structure of philanthropy but to its vanity — to the impudence of those who expect public decoration for private trifles.
'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?' — that's not a radical; that's a plain-spoken Englishman who knows the difference between giving and performing.
And in that respect, early Boffin — the genuine article — is the novel's most reliable moral compass.
Which makes his apparent fall all the more theatrical — and all the more effective as the instrument of Bella's cure.
She hears her own half-formed philosophy of money given back to her in the mouth of a man she once admired — and it sounds monstrous.
That is a piece of dramatic irony Dickens manages with extraordinary economy — no speeches about Bella's growth, just one stuttered word: 'R—r—rich!'
And the mirror cracks.
The mirror cracks — and what's left is a Bella who must choose between the lesson she's been given and the life she actually wants.
That question — what Bella chooses, and whether Dickens earns that choice — will bring us to our next section.
But for now — a genuine tension has been named, and I think Edmund has identified it most precisely: is the Boffin stratagem a moral triumph, or does it cheat the novel's own moral logic?
We'll pursue that — and Bella's final reckoning — after the break.

segments.title: A Golden Dustman: Boffin's Rise and the Corruption Question

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the river and its secrets, with the Veneerings and their mercenary salon.
Today we turn to the man at the novel's peculiar moral centre — Nicodemus Boffin, the Golden Dustman.

A man who inherits a fortune built on dust, moves into an aristocratic mansion that doesn't suit him, and finds himself besieged almost immediately by every species of parasite the Victorian world can produce.
With me today are three readers who I think will have very different things to say about what Dickens is doing here.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley, novelist and critic, who is never happier than when she can show us the machinery behind the magic.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who will remind us, as he always does, that fiction is ultimately about character and moral life rather than social programme.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the man who has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive — who hears this prose in a way the rest of us can only aspire to.
Let's begin with Boffin's arrival in his new world.
What strikes me first about the Boffin passages is how Dickens deploys the narrator as a kind of ironic impresario.
He introduces Boffin with this marvellous double-barrelled phrase —
'The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
And then immediately withdraws the sting: 'or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire.'
It's a tiny structural joke, but it tells you everything about Dickens's method in this section.
He gives you the satirical vantage and then steps back from it — just enough to let us warm to Boffin as a human being even while we're laughing at his situation.
And then there is that extraordinary simile about the house being like an aristocratic family cheese.
'Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.'
The cheese! It's absurd and perfect — the aristocratic mansion as something over-aged, over-large, teeming with life that feeds off it.
Eleanor, that cheese is one of the great comic images in the novel, and I say that as someone who has had to read it aloud many times.
You can feel the audience laughing in it — a live audience, a serial readership.
But what I find even more theatrically brilliant is the charity letter sequence.
Dickens actually performs a letter — he steps into the Duke of Linseed's voice and gives you the whole lithographed form.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six adjectives before the noun — every one of them doing satirical work.
The postscript is the killer — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.'
A duke who calls himself your 'faithful servant' — and then hits you with the fee in the postscript.
The comedy is beautifully done — Oliver is quite right on that count.
But I think we should be careful not to flatten what Dickens is doing into mere social satire.
Burke observed that hypocrisy is the tribute vice pays to virtue.
What Dickens anatomises in these letters is not simply a corrupt class — it is a corrupt moral imagination.
Every single correspondent in that catalogue — the duke, the wives, the inspired beggars — has dressed selfishness in the language of virtue.
And the really devastating passage, to my mind, is the line about documents.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That is a moral observation, not merely a comic one.
To call a scrap a document is to lie to yourself about what you are doing.
Edmund, I think that's exactly right — and it connects to something remarkable about the structure of these begging letters as a sequence.
Dickens builds a taxonomy — corporate beggars, then individual beggars, then category after category within the individual beggars.
Daughters of general officers, wives keeping secrets from husbands, husbands keeping secrets from wives, the inspired beggars, the nobly independent ones.
The list form is itself a satirical device — it says: this is infinite, there is no end to it, this is the shape of the world Boffin has entered.
And then the beggars on horseback — ready to gallop to fortune but wanting a violin or an astronomical telescope to do it.
The precision of those objects is glorious.
That precision — Eleanor, it's what makes him actable, isn't it.
Not 'a musical instrument.' A violin.
Not 'a scientific device.' An electrifying machine.
The specificity makes you hear the letter — you can almost feel the slightly sweating hand that wrote it.
And then there's the suicidal beggar with his memorandum — 'a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday.'
The comedy there is very dark, very precise, and very Victorian.
It tells you that even despair has been bureaucratised.
Which brings us, I think, to the real question about Boffin — not about the beggars who circle him, but about what money actually does to him.
We have a will — or the suggestion of one — reading that old Harmon intended his fortune very coldly.
Wegg reads out the supposed earlier document with what one can only call theatrical relish.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him' — that is a sentence designed to wound.
It is the bequest of a man who dispensed not only fortune but judgment.
And Boffin's willingness to inhabit that judgment — to be content with his cheese-mansion and his parasites — says something rather important about his character.
And into that moral landscape steps Silas Wegg — who is the novel's most vivid portrait of what happens when power meets a base nature.
There's a passage that I find almost frightening in its clarity about this.
'Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures.'
Dickens goes on: Wegg hovers over Boffin's house with 'his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards.'
That is the novel's anatomy of villainy stated almost as a theorem.
Power divorced from intellect or virtue doesn't elevate — it merely feeds the worst in whoever holds it.
The phrase 'Evil Genius' that Dickens uses for Wegg in that same passage — that is an actor's gift.
'Hovering over Mr Boffin's house in the superior character of its Evil Genius.'
'Superior character' — Wegg has cast himself in a role.
He is performing villainy for his own gratification as much as for any material gain.
And Dickens lets us see the smallness of it — a man with a wooden leg prowling a street corner, drunk on imaginary power.
It is pathetic and sinister at once, which is the precise tone Dickens always manages with his best grotesques.
And Boffin himself stands in contrast to all of this — Wegg, the charitable parasites, the ducal letterwriters.
The novel's corruption question — whether the dust heaps corrupt their inheritor — is posed around a man who is, at this stage, genuinely good-natured.
He regards the parasitic expense of his mansion as a sort of — and I love this — 'perpetual Legacy Duty.'
That is the response of a man who accepts the world as it is without being diminished by it.
The question the novel is really posing is not whether money corrupts in the abstract, but whether this particular man — with his particular virtues — will hold.
Edmund frames it perfectly — and it's a question the novel will take a very long time to answer, in ways none of us quite expected.

What we've seen today is the remarkable range Dickens deploys in establishing this world: the satirical taxonomy of the letters, the grotesque comedy of the parasitic mansion, the cold judgment embedded in the will, and Wegg lurking in the dark with his borrowed power.
All of it circling Boffin — who remains, for now, oddly serene at the centre of it.
In our next segment, we'll look at what happens when Boffin begins to change — or appears to.
Do join us.

segments.title: The Man in the Dark: Harmon's Secret and the Novel's Architecture

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the series working its way through every layer of Dickens's last completed novel.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers, each bringing a different lens to this extraordinary book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher whose great gift is making the craft of fiction feel like the most urgent thing in the world.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads every novel as a moral drama — a test of individual character against circumstance.
And Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he hears what the prose is doing before he sees it on the page.
Today's segment sits at the very architecture of the novel: Harmon's secret, his disguise, and the extraordinary web of loyalty and deception Dickens builds around it.
Eleanor, the Boffins — their loyalty to young John Harmon, their resistance to old Harmon's cruelty — that's where this whole moral structure begins, isn't it?
It really is — and what strikes me immediately is how Dickens chooses to give us this backstory through Boffin's own voice, in all its glorious idiosyncrasy.
This isn't the narrator summarising the past — it's a man reliving it, and the difference is everything.
Listen to how Boffin describes the old man's rages — Dickens gives him this almost parenthetical precision about Mrs Boffin's bonnet.
'she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head'
That little aside — parenthetical, affectionate, utterly specific — is doing enormous work.
It tells us Boffin sees his wife with tender exactness, even inside a story about violence.
And then comes the ending — 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.' — that repetition is pure theatrical shock.
'Dropped her.' — I mean, you simply cannot improve on that.
As a performer, the moment I encounter a sentence fragment like that, I know Dickens is writing for the voice.
There's a beat — a full stop in the thought — and then he says it again, half a second later, quieter.
The repetition isn't for emphasis — it's for the character processing what he just said, what he once witnessed.
Boffin is a great comic figure, but in that moment Dickens grants him a grief that is absolutely unshowy and absolutely real.
What moves me, I confess, is the moral weight Dickens assigns to this loyalty — and how quietly he does it.
The Boffins are not educated people making refined ethical choices — they are honest and true, as the narrator puts it, by nature.
And what is remarkable — genuinely remarkable — is that old Harmon, that inveterate misanthrope, could perceive it.
Dickens writes, with considerable precision, that old Harmon had perceived
'the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt'
Wealth confronted by virtue, and wealth found wanting — that is the oldest moral drama in literature, and Dickens handles it with perfect economy here.
Edmund, that phrase — 'his stony heart' — I find it fascinating that Dickens uses a cliché there, deliberately, I think.
The narrator calls old Harmon 'the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail' — which is one of those compressed metaphors Dickens buries in subordinate clauses as if they cost him nothing.
The house is a jail, the father is its jailer — and even in death the metaphor holds, because his will imprisons everyone who survives him.
That's the architecture I find so thrilling — metaphor and plot are doing exactly the same work at the same moment.
And then we arrive at the scene with Wegg, which is — I'll say it — one of the most satisfying villain-undoing sequences Dickens ever wrote.
Harmon grabs Wegg, knocks his head against the wall, and then — while physically holding him — delivers this extraordinary speech.
The comedy and the menace are completely inseparable.
He says, with what Dickens calls 'the heartiest good will,'
'I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.'
'The heartiest good will' — that's Dickens's comic timing at its most precise.
The violence is real — and yet the phrase describing it is warmly domestic.
I shall confess that I take that scene somewhat more seriously than Oliver does, though I enjoy his reading.
Because the Dutch bottle and its contents — that is where justice is actually dispensed, and it matters enormously.
Harmon tells Wegg what that document actually contained — and I think the language deserves to be heard carefully.
'That Dutch bottle contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father.'
'Unhappy self-tormenting father' — that is a man receiving his moral verdict in a subordinate clause, without ceremony.
And the will's exclusion of both children — one already dead of a broken heart — represents the elder Harmon's final, futile act of cruelty.
What Edmund identifies there leads me to something structurally remarkable about this whole sequence.
Boffin buried that bottle — not to profit from it, but because it slurred the memory of two children he loved.
That is a wholly disinterested moral act — one that cost him and could only benefit others.
And then the surveillance of Wegg — Harmon tells him they knew, and watched, and waited to maximise his fall.
Dickens builds this counter-conspiracy with genuine structural pleasure — Sloppy as Wegg's unwitting shadow, Venus as the informant.
And Harmon announces this counter-conspiracy with such controlled relish — he says, literally, that it was designed so that Wegg's disappointment might be the heaviest possible.
He telegraphs the whole scheme — he wants Wegg to understand exactly how thoroughly he was outmanoeuvred.
Harmon says, holding him at arm's length — one can picture the scene exactly —
'I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.'
'The chief occupation and delight of his life' — applied to following a one-legged ballad-seller around a dust-yard.
Dickens's comedy never loses its target — Wegg is absurd, and the machinery deployed against him is proportionally absurd.
What I hear across all of this is a novel where the hidden — identity, will, loyalty — is the engine, and revelation is the reward.
Harmon's secret doesn't just drive the plot — it holds the novel's moral world together, as Eleanor, Edmund, and Oliver have each shown us in different ways.
In our next segment, we turn to another kind of disguise entirely — the performance of wealth, and what Dickens makes of the dust-heaps as legacy.

segments.title: Dickens on Display: Comic Monsters and the Art of Exaggeration

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — and marvel at how the pieces fit together.
Today's segment is called Dickens on Display: Comic Monsters and the Art of Exaggeration.
And we have three remarkable company to pull it apart with me.
Dr Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and writes novels herself — she is our guide to how Dickens builds his effects from the inside out, sentence by sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads every novel as a story about moral character — and who keeps us honest when readings become too convenient.
And Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive, and brings to this novel the ear of a born performer.
Oliver, let's begin with you, because comedy is your natural habitat — and Our Mutual Friend opens its comic account very early, with a scene so absurd it could almost be Chaplin.
The scene at Betty Higden's doorway is a small masterpiece of physical comedy, and Dickens knows exactly what he's doing.
You have a chubby orphan, a dangerous board across the doorway, and two rather dignified visitors — all the ingredients for magnificent chaos.
But the stroke of genius is in the prose itself.
Dickens writes:
'Being an orphan of a chubby conformation, he then took to rolling, and had rolled into the gutter before they could come up.'
'A chubby conformation' — that is the phrase of a comic genius who has studied exactly how to make you picture the thing while simultaneously making you laugh at the vocabulary used to describe it.
And then the poor child rolls — he doesn't fall, he doesn't stumble — he rolls, as orphans of a chubby conformation naturally do.
What I love about that sentence is the passive innocence of it — as if rolling into the gutter were simply the orphan's natural destiny, something gravity had arranged.
But notice what Dickens layers on top of the slapstick — the arrival of Rokesmith and Mrs Boffin into this chaos creates an immediate social embarrassment.
He writes that they find themselves in possession — and then that qualifying phrase — 'one would say at first sight unlawful possession' — of the orphan, upside down and purple.
The narrator winks at us there — 'one would say at first sight' — that little legalistic qualification is Dickens in pure playful mode.
And the comedy snowballs — the board trips everyone, the orphan cries, and the situation acquires what Dickens calls a 'lugubrious and inhuman character.'
He gives the crying baby a critical review, essentially — 'lugubrious and inhuman.' Even the tears are absurdist.
I don't dispute any of that — the comedy is superb, and Dickens's command of bathos is beyond argument.
But I think we should not miss what the comedy is in service of — which is the introduction of Betty Higden and the world she inhabits.
The slapstick disarms us, makes us laugh — and then Dickens very quietly positions characters of quite different social standing in an absurdly equal predicament.
The board trips both the poor washerwoman and the philanthropist's wife — comedy as a small democracy of embarrassment.
Dickens's genius, which I think is fundamentally moral, operates most freely when it is most apparently frivolous.
Edmund makes a point I genuinely hadn't framed that way — comedy as a small democracy — and I think that is exactly right.
Now, if we want sheer comic mechanism at its most naked, I must insist on the scene with Wegg and Venus.
These two are already a glorious double act — the wooden-legged literary fraud and the melancholy articulator of bones.
And Dickens gives us a sentence that builds like a piece of music, until the whole thing topples.

'On the way to this crisis Mr Wegg's wooden leg had gradually elevated itself more and more, and he had nudged Mr Venus with his opposite elbow deeper and deeper, until at length the preservation of his balance became incompatible with the two actions, and he now dropped over sideways upon that gentleman, squeezing him against the settle's edge.'
The accumulation of that sentence — 'more and more,' 'deeper and deeper' — it is a comic countdown, and you know exactly when the punchline is coming, but it still lands perfectly.
And then the aftermath: 'both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon.' Four words that are as good as anything in English comic prose.
'Pecuniary swoon' — it is perfect because it fuses the physical and the financial into a single ridiculous image.
These two men are so consumed by greed that it actually renders them unconscious — the body surrenders to avarice.
But I want to press on Oliver's point about the sentence structure, because it is doing something very deliberate.

The wooden leg elevates — this gorgeous detail that the leg acts almost independently — and the elbowing gets deeper, and the two movements are building toward an inevitable catastrophe that the syntax enacts.
Dickens writes the fall into the sentence before Wegg physically falls — the sentence is itself losing balance.
Wegg is a character I find rather more troubling than funny, if I'm honest.
He is a study in the particular corruption of a man who has some education but no virtue — and Dickens understands that combination intimately.
The comedy of the swoon is brilliant — I grant that freely — but what we are watching is two men prostrated by cupidity.
Dr Johnson would have recognised the type at once — and found the farce entirely appropriate to the subject.
That tension — between comedy and moral diagnosis — seems to sit at the very centre of how Dickens uses exaggeration.
But the novel also gives us moments where comedy and tenderness become genuinely inseparable — and Oliver, I believe you've been waiting to get to the Boffin chapters.
I have been waiting — because Mrs Boffin's great speech wrapping up the secret of John Harmon is one of the finest things in the novel.
It is a speech that could belong to farce — the breathless storytelling, the repeated refrain — but it earns its emotion completely.
The rhythm of it is everything — and Dickens gives us a repeated phrase that builds to something unexpectedly moving.
'She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer.'
That phrase — 'I can't afford to be rich yet' — arrives three times in the speech, and each time Bella has done something else to earn John's delay.
It is comic in structure — the refrain, the accumulation, the absurd reverse logic of a man who refuses wealth because his wife is too good.
And yet it is one of the most genuinely romantic things in Dickens — the idea that her goodness outweighs gold.
What strikes me about that refrain is how it reverses the novel's central obsession with money.

This entire novel is saturated with people who will do anything to be rich — Wegg, the Veneerings, Lammle — and here is a man who keeps postponing wealth because being rich would interrupt something more valuable.
Dickens gives Mrs Boffin the voice of a music-hall narrator — the breathless 'then... then... then' — but the content is quietly radical.
And then the speech ends: 'and God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all' — pure Dickens, unashamed, and it works because Mrs Boffin has earned every syllable.
I want to come in here, because I think Mrs Boffin is one of the genuinely good people in the novel — and Dickens lavishes on her a kind of prose she entirely deserves.
Her speech has that quality one finds in certain figures in Fielding — an unsophisticated goodness of heart that puts sophisticated wickedness entirely to shame.
And the moment that follows — where Bella kneels at Mr Boffin's feet — is the moral centre of the whole concluding movement.
And that moment is where Dickens does something remarkable — he lets Bella's comic breathlessness carry the full weight of her moral transformation.
She hands the baby to John — 'the Inexhaustible,' Dickens calls it — and then kneels beside old Boffin.
And then comes this torrent of 'please' — the word of a child asking forgiveness, combined with the crowing triumph of someone who has finally understood.
'Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
Every 'please' is simultaneously a plea and a proclamation — it is the funniest and most affecting use of the word I know in all of Dickens.
And 'for one single minute' — that final flourish — is Bella the performer, the sparkling girl, all the way through to her redemption.
Bella forcing Boffin to turn his face to hers is the image that undoes me every time — 'she struggled with him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers.'
'His delighted face' — Dickens saves that adjective for the very moment of revelation.
Boffin has been performing cruelty for chapters and chapters — and all along, behind the performance, was a delighted face waiting to be turned toward hers.
That is the structural payoff of the whole Boffin subplot — and Dickens delivers it in a single adjective.
Eleanor is right about the adjective — and I would say it illustrates what distinguishes Dickens from all imitators.
The exaggeration, the grotesquerie, the farce — these are all preparations for a moment of absolute emotional clarity.
Bella kneeling, an exultant ringing laugh on her lips, forcing a delighted face toward hers — that is not sentimentality.
That is Dickens at his most serious — using comedy as a ladder to reach something he could not reach by direct emotional address.
A ladder to reach something he could not reach directly — that is a formulation I think we should carry with us through everything else we discuss today.
From the orphan rolling in the gutter to Bella's exultant 'please,' Dickens's comedy is never mere entertainment — it is moral imagination wearing a jester's hat.
We'll be back after a short break to follow the dust-mounds further — and to ask what all that wealth, and all that rubbish, actually means.

segments.title: Weaving Fates: How Dickens Binds Three Lives Together

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great final completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
I'm joined today by three guests who bring very different eyes to the same pages.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads for craft — for the hidden architecture inside a sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's true subject is always individual moral character — not social machinery.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more classic novels aloud than perhaps anyone alive — hears Dickens as a performer first.
Today's segment is about how Dickens weaves three very different lives — Twemlow, Bradley Headstone, Rogue Riderhood — into a single, tightening pattern.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — and with a character who seems, on the surface, almost too slight to matter.
Twemlow is one of those characters who repays close attention precisely because he appears not to repay it at all.
Dickens introduces him as, and I quote directly —
"an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use."
Now, that is not merely a comic simile — it is a moral diagnosis delivered in the key of comedy.
Twemlow is stored away when not needed, like furniture — his entire social existence is instrumental.
And then comes the line that still makes me catch my breath —
"the more Twemlow was pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other."
The higher his social utility, the more marginal his actual presence.
What strikes me about that passage is the sustained commitment to the conceit — Dickens doesn't drop the metaphor after one paragraph, he extends it with complete structural logic.
The leaves, the pulling out to twenty leaves, the Veneerings facing each other in the centre — every detail of a real dining table is pressed into service.
That technical thoroughness is what separates a great comic metaphor from a merely clever one.
And it seeds, very quietly, the novel's central question: which people are treated as ends in themselves, and which as furniture?
When I first read that passage aloud, I had to stop — because the comic rhythm demands a kind of deadpan perfection.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The name Snigsworth is doing quiet, beautiful work there — it punctures the entire pretension of the aristocracy in two syllables.
But what arrests me is how the comedy doesn't protect Twemlow from our sympathy.
You laugh, and then immediately you feel the pathos of the man stored in Duke Street when not in use.
Twemlow, then, as both comic object and quiet moral touchstone — furniture that has feelings.
But let's move to a very different kind of interiority — Bradley Headstone, and the psychological state Dickens describes in Chapter fifty-seven.
Edmund, you've been sitting with this passage — what does Dickens do here that goes beyond simple villainy?
Dickens understood something about the unrepentant that most novelists — most moralists, frankly — prefer to ignore.
Remorse, at least, is a form of moral engagement — it acknowledges the wrong and the victim.
But what does one do with a nature that refuses remorse entirely?
Dickens's answer is this —
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
Providence, you might say, will not be cheated — it simply substitutes a more refined instrument of punishment.
The sullen soul that refuses to be broken by guilt is broken instead by its own obsessive competence.
What astonishes me about that passage is the way Dickens shifts into what feels almost like a case study — a forensic register.
The narrator moves from Bradley specifically to the general category of murderer — "in the defensive declarations and pretended confessions of murderers."
And then that extraordinary phrase: "the state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times instead of once."
The punishment is aesthetic as much as moral — it's the horror of the perfectionist trapped forever refining an act that cannot be changed.
That's a very modern piece of psychological insight — and it arrives in what is ostensibly a Victorian sensation plot.
When you read it aloud, that passage has a peculiar rhythm — almost incantatory.
"Incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently" — the repetition of "doing" is not accidental.
It mimics the very compulsion it describes — the prose enacts the torture.
I've read a great deal of crime fiction over the years, and I don't think anyone has written a more chilling portrait of the unregenerate criminal mind.
The unregenerate mind — which brings us, rather neatly, to Charley Hexam and his extraordinary speech to Bradley in the same chapter.
Edmund, you've been quiet about Charley — and I suspect deliberately so.
Charley Hexam is one of Dickens's most unsettling achievements — a young man whose every instinct is for respectability, and whose every moral sense is therefore corrupted by selfishness.
He berates Bradley — and the charge he levels is one of the most damning in the novel.
"You are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me."
The irony, of course, is magnificent — Charley accuses Bradley of selfishness while making his argument entirely about the injury to Charley himself.
Two solipsists locked in mutual recrimination — neither capable of seeing the third party, which is Lizzie.
And notice the structure of Charley's speech — it's laid out like a prosecutor's indictment, very nearly point by point.
"You did see her... I confided in you... You fell in love with her... I favoured you... She could not be induced to favour you..."
Each clause is another charge — the syntax itself performs the accumulation of grievance.
But what the syntax cannot hide — and what the reader catches even when Charley does not — is that every grievance is entirely self-referential.
Playing Charley in one's head — and I have spent some time doing exactly that — you realise the speech has a kind of horrible energy.
He is genuinely aggrieved, genuinely articulate, and entirely wrong — and he doesn't know it.
That combination — the fluent, wrongheaded accuser — is one of the great comic and tragic types in all of fiction.
And what unites Charley and Bradley, I think, is that neither of them can see Lizzie as a person — only as a position in their own story.
Which leads us to Eleanor's passage — and perhaps the most technically brilliant piece of sustained suspense in the novel.
Eleanor, Rogue Riderhood is following Bradley — but Dickens makes the following itself the subject.
What Dickens does in this passage is give Riderhood a kind of professional dignity — almost a craftsman's pride — in the act of pursuit.
The key sentence is perfectly calibrated —
"He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well."
That list — slink, skulk, dog, waylay — is pure sonic craft.
Each verb is short, dark, monosyllabic — you feel the low, crouching movement in the sound of the words themselves.
And then — "the doomed Bradley's slow conception" — six words that seal his fate with absolute economy.
"Slink and skulk and dog and waylay" — I have to say, as a reader-aloud, that sequence is an absolute gift.
It asks you to slow down, go low, almost disappear into the sentence as you say it.
And then: "He knew his calling well." — the simplicity of that after the catalogue is devastating.
Dickens writes sentences that teach you how to perform them as you read — that's a very rare talent.
What strikes me morally in that passage is the inversion it performs.
Riderhood is in every conventional sense the lower creature — a blackmailer, a man of no principle.
But he has mastered his trade, while Bradley — the schoolmaster, the respectable man — is exposed as a slow and clumsy amateur in the dark arts he has chosen.
Dickens is always suspicious of respectability — and here, respectability proves to be not only hollow but incompetent.
Respectability hollow and incompetent — which is, in its way, the perfect summary of so much of what this novel is doing.
Twemlow stored in Duke Street, Bradley reliving his crime with obsessive precision, Riderhood slinking through the dark with professional ease — three lives, three registers, one tightening world.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the river — not as backdrop, but as the novel's true protagonist.
We've arrived at our final stretch, and it feels right to end where the novel itself insists on ending — with the possibility of redemption.
Our Mutual Friend is saturated in waste and corruption, but Dickens refuses to leave us there.
Three passages today ask us to look closely at how characters are remade — or how they were broken in the first place.

Eleanor, I want to start with you — because you've brought us a passage that is, on the surface, pure comedy, and yet it says something devastating about how identity gets assigned before a life even begins.
Yes — and this is one of those passages where Dickens's comedy is doing extraordinarily precise structural work.
Eugene is describing his father — M. R. F., the Most Respected Father — as a man who allocates destinies to children before they've drawn breath.
And the genius of it is that the comedy comes from the gap between pronouncement and reality — every single time.
Listen to how Dickens lands this — Eugene says, with perfect deadpan affection:
A very shaky one.
Three words, and the whole social edifice comes down.
What Dickens is really doing here is showing us the tyranny of the predetermined self — identity as something imposed rather than grown.
And Eugene, crucially, survives it — survives M. R. F. — precisely by treating the whole arrangement with amused detachment.
I have to say, performing that passage is an absolute gift.
The rhythm of it — Dickens writes the pause into the grammar.
That italicised "Was born" — it's a full stop masquerading as a sentence.
You deliver it flat, and then you let the audience catch up to the joke.
But Eleanor is right that there's something serious underneath it — Eugene is a man who has never been allowed to be surprised by his own life.
Which is precisely why, later in the novel, the fact that Lizzie genuinely astonishes him is so transformative.

One might observe that M. R. F. is not so very different from a great many Victorian fathers — or indeed from the Victorian social order itself, which likewise dispensed roles by birth rather than by temperament.
But I think the passage's real interest is moral rather than sociological.
Eugene's detachment — charming as it is — has been a form of evasion for most of the novel.
His wit is a defence against commitment of any kind — professional, emotional, moral.
Dr Johnson observed that no man is a hypocrite in his pleasures — and Eugene has constructed his entire life on pleasures precisely because they ask nothing of him.
His redemption, when it comes, is genuinely earned — but one should not mistake the diagnosis for the cure.
That tension between wit as evasion and wit as survival runs through so much of this novel.
But Eugene's comfortable irony is a world away from the circumstances of our next passage — which brings us to a child who has no such armour at all.
Oliver, Lizzie Hexam's words here are very nearly unbearable — tell us why.
They are unbearable — and that's precisely deliberate.
Lizzie is speaking to her brother Charley, and the restraint of the telling is what makes it devastating.
She says of this poor child:
And then that parenthetical — "if she ever had one" — lands like a quietly placed stone.
Dickens doesn't shout it.
He tucks it into the grammar of the sentence — and it's all the more damning for that.
That parenthetical is doing enormous work — it's the novel's social conscience compressed into a single clause.
What strikes me is how Dickens frames the child's condition as accumulation — "surrounded by drunken people from her cradle" — it's a whole inheritance of damage.
Not one catastrophe but a slow saturation — the way poverty and drink compound one another across generations.
And Lizzie sees this with absolute clarity — which is part of why she is one of the novel's most morally lucid characters.
She has come from the water's edge — from degradation herself — and she looks at this child and sees what she might have been.
One resists the temptation to read this passage as polemic — though Dickens plainly feels the injustice keenly.
What saves it, artistically, is that the voice belongs to Lizzie — a character of genuine moral seriousness — rather than to an authorial lecture.
The father, we're told, is "a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober" — but also "a good workman."
Dickens does not permit himself — or us — the comfort of simple condemnation.
That is the mark of a moralist, not merely a propagandist.
A good workman — that detail is quietly heartbreaking, and Edmund is right that it changes the moral register entirely.
Which brings us to our final passage — and I think in some ways the most remarkable in today's selection.
John Harmon, lying in a public-house bed, still officially dead — and making one of the strangest decisions in all of Victorian fiction.
Eleanor, this is yours — and I suspect you've been waiting to get to it.
I have — because structurally this passage is extraordinary.
John Harmon is narrating his own resurrection — from a hospital bed, in secret, with the whole plot of the novel hinging on what he decides next.
And what he decides is this — to stay dead, for a while, in order to understand who Bella Wilfer really is.
He tells us himself:
That word — "proving" — is doing everything.
It carries the weight of a test, a fear, and a hope — all at once.
And notice how Dickens roots it — "the moral timidity that dates from my childhood with my poor sister" — this is not romantic melodrama; it's a psychologically precise account of damage.
I find this one of the most morally interesting passages in the novel — and also one of the most quietly uncomfortable.
Because Harmon's decision is, on one level, a deception — he is testing a woman without her knowledge or consent.
And yet Dickens asks us to sympathise — and largely succeeds — because the motivation is so plainly rooted in genuine dread.
"The fate that they should lead to nothing but evil" — his father's wealth is not a blessing but an inheritance of corruption.
What Harmon wants is to be loved as a man, not as a fortune.
That is not an ignoble aspiration — even if the method is, shall we say, morally adventurous.
"Morally adventurous" — Edmund, I shall be borrowing that phrase.
But he's right — and what I find extraordinary as a performer is how Dickens handles the voice in this confession.
Harmon is speaking in retrospect, in private — it reads almost like a man thinking aloud to himself.
"I am sure it was while I lay in that bed there" — that "there" is extraordinary; it reaches back through memory as if the bed were still present.
It's the grammar of trauma — the way certain moments refuse to become past tense.
And that refusal — that insistence on remaining in the wreckage until the truth is known — is what connects all three passages today.
Remaining in the wreckage until the truth is known — that's the thesis of this novel, in a sentence.
Eugene surviving M. R. F.'s destiny for him by learning to be astonished.
A child surrounded by ruin, seen and named with terrible clarity by Lizzie Hexam.
And John Harmon, choosing to stay dead because the living world has never yet shown him it could be trusted.
What Dickens asks of all of them — and of us — is exactly what Oliver said: to refuse the past tense until something genuine has been proved.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan — three guides through this extraordinary, inexhaustible novel.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked will return.

Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.

The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential

c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’
c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.
c42:p162.best_quote: I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an

c38:p47.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically advises Bella to pursue money above all else, declaring that she should capitalize on her beauty and the wealth they will bestow on her to become and remain rich.

‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
